entry.title: From Jenkins pipelines to GitHub Actions - a mapping, not a migration guide

link.title: From Jenkins pipelines to GitHub Actions - a mapping, not a migration guide

entry.content:
I have written a lot of Jenkins - shared libraries, Job DSL seed jobs, declarative pipelines, the works - and over the last years most of it has moved to GitHub Actions. Every migration guide I read was either “here is how to export your jobs” (you cannot, not meaningfully) or a sales pitch. What I actually wanted was a dictionary: I know what this Jenkins thing does, what is the Actions word for it, and where does the mental model break. So here is that dictionary, with the one place where Actions is genuinely better and the two places where you will miss Jenkins.

The dictionary

Jenkins GitHub Actions Notes
Jenkinsfile .github/workflows/*.yml one file per workflow, several workflows per repo
pipeline { stages { stage {} } } jobs: → steps: a job is the unit of parallelism and of the runner
agent { label 'linux' } runs-on: ubuntu-latest labels still exist, for self-hosted runners
steps { sh '...' } - run: ... multi-line with run: \|
when { branch 'main' } if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' on job or step
parallel { } strategy: matrix: or multiple jobs matrix is the idiomatic one
post { always { } } if: always() on a step failure(), success(), cancelled() too
parameters { } on: workflow_dispatch: inputs: typed: string, choice, boolean
triggers { cron('H 2 * * *') } on: schedule: - cron: '17 2 * * *' no H, pick an odd minute yourself
environment { } env: workflow, job or step scope
credentials('id') $ plus OIDC, see below
lock('deploy-prod') concurrency: group: deploy-prod cancel-in-progress optional
input message: 'Deploy?' environment: with required reviewers approval lives in repo settings
archiveArtifacts / stash actions/upload-artifact / download-artifact artifacts cross jobs; stash was within a build
shared library vars/*.groovy composite action or reusable workflow the big one, next section
Job DSL seed job reusable workflow with on: workflow_call plus a template repo
buildDiscarder(logRotator(...)) repository settings → retention not in YAML
Jenkins agents self-hosted runners or just use hosted ones

Shared libraries → composite actions and reusable workflows

This is where the model actually differs, so it is worth more than a table row.

A Jenkins shared library is Groovy code: it can have functions, classes, loops, and a vars/deploy.groovy step that takes a map of arguments and does anything. Actions has no scripting layer in YAML. Instead you get two composition tools, and you pick by granularity:

Composite action = a reusable step sequence. Lives in action.yml, takes inputs, produces outputs, runs inside the calling job on the calling runner. This is the replacement for the typical vars/tofuPlan.groovy:

# .github/actions/tofu-plan/action.yml
name: tofu plan
inputs:
  working-directory:
    required: true
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: opentofu/setup-opentofu@v1
    - run: tofu init -input=false
      shell: bash
      working-directory: $
    - run: tofu plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      shell: bash
      working-directory: $

Reusable workflow = a reusable job set. Triggered with on: workflow_call, called from another workflow with uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/plan.yml@main, runs as its own jobs with its own runners. This is the replacement for the Job DSL seed job that stamped out one pipeline per service: one reusable workflow in a central repo, each service repo has a five-line workflow that calls it.

The thing you lose is logic. There is no if (env == 'prod') { ... } else { ... } in a composite action, only if: expressions on steps. In practice that pushed me to move logic out of CI into scripts and Makefiles in the repo, which is where it should have been in the first place. Jenkins let you hide a lot of real program in a vars/ folder.

The place Actions is better: credentials via OIDC

In Jenkins the AWS credentials for deploying were an access key and secret stored in the credentials store, rotated when someone remembered. Actions can skip the long-lived key entirely. The job requests an OIDC token from GitHub, and AWS trusts GitHub’s identity provider for a specific repository and branch:

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-actions-plan
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/tofu-plan
        with:
          working-directory: envs/prod

The IAM role’s trust policy restricts token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub to repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main, or to an environment. No secret exists anywhere. A leaked workflow log cannot leak a key because there is no key. This alone was worth the migration for the infrastructure repos.

A full example, side by side

The pipeline every infrastructure team has - fmt, validate, plan on pull requests:

// Jenkinsfile
pipeline {
  agent { label 'linux' }
  options { timeout(time: 20, unit: 'MINUTES') }
  stages {
    stage('fmt')      { steps { sh 'tofu fmt -check -recursive' } }
    stage('validate') { steps { sh 'tofu init -backend=false && tofu validate' } }
    stage('plan') {
      when { changeRequest() }
      steps {
        withCredentials([aws(credentialsId: 'aws-plan')]) {
          sh 'tofu init -input=false && tofu plan -input=false'
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

# .github/workflows/tofu.yml
name: tofu
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: tofu-$
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: opentofu/setup-opentofu@v1
      - run: tofu fmt -check -recursive
      - run: tofu init -backend=false && tofu validate

  plan:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    needs: check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-actions-plan
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/tofu-plan
        with:
          working-directory: envs/prod

Roughly the same length. The Actions version has the OIDC role instead of a stored credential, concurrency instead of hoping two PR builds do not race on the same state lock, and needs: making the dependency explicit instead of implied by stage order.

The two things you will miss

The Blue Ocean / stage view. Actions shows jobs as a graph and steps as a log. It does not show stages within a job visually, and a forty-step job is a forty-section log. You adapt by making more, smaller jobs, which also parallelises better, but the first week feels like flying blind.

Running the pipeline locally. A Jenkinsfile could, with effort, be replayed. Actions workflows run on GitHub, full stop. act exists and gets you most of the way for simple workflows, but OIDC, environments and anything touching github.* context behave differently. The practical answer was the same as for the logic question: put the real work in scripts that run with no CI at all, and keep the YAML to orchestration. If the YAML is boring enough that you never need to run it locally, you have done it right.

Pin your actions

Last thing, because it is a security issue and not a style one. uses: some-org/some-action@v4 follows a moving tag. If that repository is compromised, your workflow runs the attacker’s code with your OIDC token. Pin to a commit SHA with the version as a comment, and let Dependabot bump it:

- uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e3dd6a429d7300a6a4c196c26e071d42e0343502 # v4.0.2

Jenkins had this problem too, with plugins, it just was less visible. In Actions the supply chain is in the YAML where you can see it, so there is no excuse.

What I actually wanted was a dictionary: I know what this Jenkins thing does, what is the Actions word for it, and where does the mental model break. So here is that dictionary, with the one place where Actions is genuinely better and the two places where you will miss Jenkins.

entry.title: Podman on macOS instead of Docker Desktop - what actually changes

link.title: Podman on macOS instead of Docker Desktop - what actually changes

entry.content:
My About page has said “Podman / OrbStack” instead of “Docker” for a while now, and I keep getting asked whether that is a political statement or a practical one. Practical. Docker Desktop’s licence terms made it a procurement question in a lot of companies, and once you have to justify a tool you start asking what you actually use it for. For me the answer was: run a container, build an image, occasionally a compose file. Podman does all of that. This post is the list of what is different on a Mac, because the differences are real, just smaller than the internet makes them sound.

There is still a VM, you just see it

Containers are a Linux thing. On a Mac both Docker Desktop and Podman run them inside a Linux virtual machine. Docker hides that VM completely. Podman does not:

brew install podman
podman machine init --cpus 4 --memory 8192 --disk-size 60
podman machine start

That creates a Fedora CoreOS VM (using Apple’s Virtualization framework on Apple silicon), and from then on the podman command on your Mac talks to the Podman service inside it over a socket. podman machine stop when you want your battery back. The upside of seeing the VM: you decide how big it is, you can podman machine ssh into it when something is weird, and you can have more than one (podman machine init work, podman machine init play).

The docker command, and the tools that hardcode it

Muscle memory and third-party tools both type docker. Two layers fix that.

For your shell, podman accepts the same subcommands and flags for the everyday stuff - run, build, ps, exec, logs, pull, push, images, rm, rmi. An alias is enough:

alias docker=podman

For tools that talk to the Docker socket rather than the CLI - Testcontainers, some IDE plugins, anything using the Docker SDK - Podman ships a helper that puts a compatible socket at the standard path:

sudo podman-mac-helper install
podman machine stop && podman machine start
ls -la /var/run/docker.sock   # -> symlink into your Podman machine's socket

After that, software that looks for /var/run/docker.sock finds a Docker-API-compatible endpoint and mostly does not notice. “Mostly” because the API compatibility is good but not total; Testcontainers works, a few niche tools that rely on Docker-only API fields do not. Setting DOCKER_HOST to the socket path, which podman machine start prints, is the alternative when the helper is not an option.

Compose

podman compose exists and is a thin wrapper: it looks for docker-compose or podman-compose on your PATH and runs that against the Podman socket. So the realistic setup is:

brew install docker-compose    # the Compose v2 binary, no Docker Desktop needed
podman compose up -d

Compose files I use day to day work unchanged. The things that have bitten people are network_mode: host (not meaningful on a Mac with either tool), and anything mounting the Docker socket into a container, which needs the Podman socket path instead.

Rootless by default, and what that means on a Mac

Podman’s headline feature is rootless containers. On the Mac this is slightly confusing: the VM is yours, so what does rootless even mean? It means the Podman service inside the VM runs as an unprivileged user, so a container breakout lands in a user account inside a VM, not in root inside a VM. Practically, two consequences:

  • binding ports below 1024 works anyway, because the VM is configured to allow it,
  • a handful of images that insist on doing privileged things at start (some older database images, anything that wants to mount) fail. For those, podman machine set --rootful switches the machine to rootful mode, and you are back to Docker-equivalent behaviour.

I run rootless and have flipped exactly one machine to rootful, for one project. The default is right.

Volumes and file sharing

Bind-mounting a directory from the Mac into a container goes Mac → VM → container, and the Mac → VM hop is the historically slow part, on both tools. Podman uses virtiofs for it now, which is fine for source code and config, and painful for the same thing it is painful for everywhere: node_modules with sixty thousand files, or a database data directory. The fix is the same as on Docker: keep heavy data in a named volume (podman volume create), which lives on the VM’s disk, and bind-mount only what you edit.

Images and registries

Pulls from Docker Hub need the full name or a configured search list. podman pull nginx asks which registry you mean; podman pull docker.io/library/nginx does not. Add docker.io to unqualified-search-registries in ~/.config/containers/registries.conf and short names work again. Not a Mac thing, but it is the first thing everyone hits.

Builds are done by Buildah under the hood, and podman build -f Dockerfile . reads a Dockerfile unchanged. Multi-arch builds for pushing an arm64 image to be run on amd64 EC2 are podman build --platform linux/amd64, with the usual emulation slowness.

Where OrbStack comes in

OrbStack is the other name on my About page. It is a commercial macOS app (free for personal use) that provides a Docker-compatible engine and lightweight Linux machines, with a focus on being fast and quiet. It is what I reach for when I want zero friction: a project with a docker-compose.yml someone else maintains, where I do not want to find out about any difference at all. Podman is what I reach for when the environment matters - when I am going to deploy to Kubernetes anyway and want the same tool that produces pods (podman generate kube, podman play kube), or on a machine where I want everything open source. Having both installed is not a conflict, they do not share a socket unless you tell them to.

Would I switch back

No, but not out of principle. The day-to-day commands are the same, the VM being visible is a feature once you get used to it, and the socket helper covers the tools that care. The friction that is left - the short-name registry prompt, the occasional image that wants rootful - is a one-time fix each. If your workflow is “compose up, write code, compose down”, the honest summary is that you will stop noticing within a week.

Docker Desktop’s licence terms made it a procurement question in a lot of companies, and once you have to justify a tool you start asking what you actually use it for. For me the answer was: run a container, build an image, occasionally a compose file. Podman does all of that. This post is the list of what is different on a Mac, because the differences are real, just smaller than the internet makes them sound.

entry.title: Go: a request ID on every log line with log/slog, without passing a logger around

link.title: Go: a request ID on every log line with log/slog, without passing a logger around

entry.content:
The single most useful field in a production log is the one that lets you pull every line belonging to one request. Most Go codebases get there by threading a *slog.Logger through every function signature, or by stuffing the logger into the context and fishing it out everywhere. There is a cleaner way that the slog design makes almost trivial: a Handler that reads the request ID from the context.Context it is given. Then every call site is just slog.InfoContext(ctx, ...), and the ID appears on its own.

The idea in one paragraph

Every slog logging method has a Context variant, slog.InfoContext(ctx, msg, attrs...), and the context is passed down to the handler’s Handle(ctx, record) method. The built-in handlers ignore it. Ours will not: it looks for a request ID in the context and, if there is one, appends it to the record before delegating to the real handler. Nobody downstream needs to know a logger exists beyond the standard package functions.

The handler

package logging

import (
	"context"
	"log/slog"
)

type ctxKey struct{}

// WithRequestID returns a context carrying the request id.
func WithRequestID(ctx context.Context, id string) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, ctxKey{}, id)
}

// RequestID returns the request id stored in ctx, or "".
func RequestID(ctx context.Context) string {
	id, _ := ctx.Value(ctxKey{}).(string)
	return id
}

// ctxHandler wraps another slog.Handler and adds request_id from the context.
type ctxHandler struct {
	slog.Handler
}

func NewHandler(inner slog.Handler) slog.Handler {
	return ctxHandler{Handler: inner}
}

func (h ctxHandler) Handle(ctx context.Context, r slog.Record) error {
	if id := RequestID(ctx); id != "" {
		r.AddAttrs(slog.String("request_id", id))
	}
	return h.Handler.Handle(ctx, r)
}

// WithAttrs and WithGroup must return the wrapper, not the inner handler,
// otherwise a logger.With(...) call silently drops the request id.
func (h ctxHandler) WithAttrs(attrs []slog.Attr) slog.Handler {
	return ctxHandler{Handler: h.Handler.WithAttrs(attrs)}
}

func (h ctxHandler) WithGroup(name string) slog.Handler {
	return ctxHandler{Handler: h.Handler.WithGroup(name)}
}

The comment on WithAttrs and WithGroup is the one non-obvious thing. slog.Handler is an interface with those two methods, and if you embed the inner handler and do not override them, logger.With("component", "db") returns a logger whose handler is the inner one, and the request ID disappears for that logger only. That bug is quiet and annoying to find. Override both, always.

Wire it up once in main:

slog.SetDefault(slog.New(logging.NewHandler(
	slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, &slog.HandlerOptions{Level: slog.LevelInfo}),
)))

HTTP: a middleware that mints or forwards the ID

func RequestIDMiddleware(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		id := r.Header.Get("X-Request-ID")
		if id == "" {
			var b [16]byte
			rand.Read(b[:]) // crypto/rand; the error is always nil on supported platforms since Go 1.24
			id = hex.EncodeToString(b[:])
		}
		w.Header().Set("X-Request-ID", id)
		ctx := logging.WithRequestID(r.Context(), id)
		next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))
	})
}

Honouring an incoming X-Request-ID means a request that crosses three services keeps one ID across all three logs, as long as each service forwards the header on outgoing calls. Returning it in the response means a user can read it from their browser’s network tab and paste it into a bug report, which is worth more than it sounds.

From here on, handlers and everything they call just do:

func (s *Server) handleOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	ctx := r.Context()
	slog.InfoContext(ctx, "order received", "customer", custID)

	if err := s.store.Save(ctx, order); err != nil {
		slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "saving order", "err", err)
		http.Error(w, "internal error", 500)
		return
	}
}

s.store.Save receives the same ctx, logs with slog.WarnContext(ctx, ...) three packages deep, and the line comes out with the same request_id. No logger parameter anywhere.

Lambda: the ID already exists

In a Lambda function the context handed to your handler already carries the invocation’s request ID. Pull it out and drop it into our context once at the top:

import "github.com/aws/aws-lambda-go/lambdacontext"

func handler(ctx context.Context, evt events.SQSEvent) error {
	if lc, ok := lambdacontext.FromContext(ctx); ok {
		ctx = logging.WithRequestID(ctx, lc.AwsRequestID)
	}
	slog.InfoContext(ctx, "batch received", "records", len(evt.Records))
	// ...
}

The nice side effect: that is the same ID CloudWatch prints in its own START RequestId: ... and REPORT lines, so your structured lines and the runtime’s lines correlate with no extra work.

Reading it back in CloudWatch

Stdout from a Lambda or an ECS task lands in CloudWatch Logs as-is, one JSON object per line. Logs Insights parses JSON automatically, so the query to follow one request is:

fields @timestamp, level, msg, err
| filter request_id = "4f1c0b2e9a7d4c3e8b6a5f0e1d2c3b4a"
| sort @timestamp asc

And the one you actually run on a bad day, “which requests errored in the last hour and how many lines did each produce”:

filter level = "ERROR"
| stats count() as lines, min(@timestamp) as first_seen by request_id
| sort first_seen desc
| limit 50

If you want this to work for ECS as well, use the awslogs log driver with no special format, JSON lines are enough.

Two things to avoid

Do not put the logger itself in the context. It works, but every call site becomes logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) and people forget, fall back to slog.Info, and the ID vanishes from exactly the lines you need. Putting only the ID in the context and having the handler do the work means the plain slog.InfoContext is the right call everywhere.

Do not forget the Context variants. slog.Info(msg) passes context.Background() to the handler, so no ID. A go vet style check for this does not exist in the standard tooling as far as I know; a grep -rn 'slog\.\(Info\|Warn\|Error\|Debug\)(' in CI is crude and effective.

The whole thing is forty lines, uses nothing outside the standard library and the Lambda SDK, and it is the first thing I add to any new Go service now. Ten minutes once, and every incident afterwards starts with a request ID instead of a timestamp and a guess.

Most Go codebases get there by threading a *slog.Logger through every function signature, or by stuffing the logger into the context and fishing it out everywhere. There is a cleaner way that the slog design makes almost trivial: a Handler that reads the request ID from the context.Context it is given. Then every call site is just slog.InfoContext(ctx, ...), and the ID appears on its own.

entry.title: Blocking egress from Lambda: the sequel to the EKS post

link.title: Blocking egress from Lambda: the sequel to the EKS post

entry.content:
After the EKS egress post the first question I got was “and what about Lambda?”. Fair. A lot of the Python glue I write runs as Lambda functions, those functions call third-party APIs, and the supply-chain argument is identical: a compromised dependency in a function has the same unrestricted internet access as one in a pod. The answer is mostly the same tool, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, with one big catch that changes the economics.

The catch: a Lambda outside a VPC is invisible to you

By default a Lambda function does not run in your VPC. It runs in an AWS-managed network with direct internet access, uses an AWS-managed resolver, and none of your VPC controls - security groups, NACLs, DNS Firewall, Network Firewall - apply to it. There is nothing to attach a rule to. For egress control, a function has to be in a VPC. Period.

Putting it there is one block:

resource "aws_lambda_function" "worker" {
  function_name = "worker"
  role          = aws_iam_role.worker.arn
  runtime       = "python3.12"
  handler       = "app.handler"
  filename      = data.archive_file.worker.output_path

  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids         = var.private_subnet_ids
    security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.worker.id]
  }
}

The function now gets elastic network interfaces in your private subnets, resolves DNS through the VPC resolver (the .2 address), and goes through your route tables. Which means two things.

Thing one: you now pay for a NAT

A function in a private subnet has no internet route unless the subnet has a NAT Gateway. If the function needs to reach the internet at all, you need one, and a NAT Gateway bills per hour and per gigabyte processed, per availability zone. For a function that previously cost a few cents a month, the NAT is now the dominant line item, in the tens of dollars a month before any traffic. That is the real price of egress control on Lambda, and it is why many teams do not do it.

Three ways to keep it reasonable:

  • One NAT, not one per AZ, for non-critical functions. You lose AZ-independence for egress, you save two thirds.
  • No internet at all if the function only talks to AWS. S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints are free; interface endpoints for other services cost per hour too, but a handful is still cheaper than a NAT with traffic, and a function with no route to the internet is the strongest egress control there is.
  • Share the VPC and NAT that your EKS cluster already has. If you did the previous post, the DNS Firewall rule group is already associated with that VPC, and a function dropped into its private subnets is covered on day one.

Thing two: DNS Firewall now applies

This is the good part. Because the function uses the VPC resolver, a DNS Firewall rule group associated with the VPC filters its DNS queries exactly like it filters a pod’s. The module from the previous post needs no change:

module "dns_firewall" {
  source = "./modules/dns-firewall"

  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
  blocked_domains = [
    "evil-domain.com",
    "definitely-not-crypto-mining.io",
  ]
  enable_query_logging = true
}

Or, if you prefer an allowlist for a function whose destinations are known - which for a Lambda is usually the case, it calls two APIs and that is it - flip it around: a rule that ALLOWs your known domains with a low priority number, then a rule that BLOCKs * after it. The previous post has both patterns.

Seeing what a function is trying to reach

Resolver query logging, pointed at a CloudWatch log group, is how you find out what to allow before you turn the block on. Each log line has the query name, the source IP and the firewall action:

fields @timestamp, srcaddr, query_name, firewall_rule_action
| filter firewall_rule_action = "BLOCK"
| stats count() by query_name, srcaddr
| sort count desc

srcaddr is the private IP of the function’s ENI. To map it back to a function, aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces with that IP returns an interface whose description starts with AWS Lambda VPC ENI and names the function. Not elegant, but you only do it while building the allowlist.

Run with firewall_rule_action = "ALERT" for a week first - the rule logs instead of blocking - then switch the rule to BLOCK. A function that silently fails because its licence-check domain got blocked is a bad Monday.

What DNS Firewall does not catch, again

Same limitation as for EKS: it filters DNS resolution, not packets. Code that connects to a hardcoded IP, or that resolves through its own DNS-over-HTTPS client, never asks the VPC resolver. For most third-party Python packages that is a theoretical problem - they use requests, requests uses the system resolver - but for a function processing untrusted input, it is a real one. The next step up is AWS Network Firewall with domain-based stateful rules, which inspects the SNI in the TLS handshake and so works on the connection itself. It is also an order of magnitude more expensive than DNS Firewall, so for Lambda I would only reach for it when the VPC already has one.

The checklist I use now

  1. Does the function need the internet at all? If not: VPC, private subnets, gateway endpoints, no NAT. Done, and it is free.
  2. If yes: VPC with existing NAT where possible, DNS Firewall rule group associated, query logging on.
  3. One week in ALERT, read the logs, write the allowlist.
  4. Switch to BLOCK, add a CloudWatch alarm on the count of blocked queries so a new dependency phoning home shows up as a page instead of a surprise.

Compared to the EKS version this is less work, because there is no cluster DNS layer in between, and more expensive, because of the NAT. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on what the function processes. For the one that parses attachments from a public inbox, yes. For the one that rotates a tag on a snapshot once a night, I leave it outside the VPC and sleep fine.
entry.summary: After the EKS egress post the first question I got was “and what about Lambda?”. Fair. The answer is mostly the same tool, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, with one big catch that changes the economics.

entry.title: Testing an OpenTofu module without an AWS account: tofu test and mock_provider

link.title: Testing an OpenTofu module without an AWS account: tofu test and mock_provider

entry.content:
In July I published a DNS Firewall module and admitted that “tested” meant “applied it once and looked”. That is how most infrastructure modules are tested, and it is why module refactors are scary. OpenTofu has had tofu test since 1.6 and provider mocking since 1.8, which together let you assert what a module does - how many rules it creates, that the action is BLOCK, that the wildcard gets added - without credentials, without a VPC, in a few seconds, in CI. Here is that module with real tests.

The shape of a test

Tests live in tests/*.tftest.hcl next to the module. Each file has run blocks, each run does a plan or an apply of the module with some variables and then checks assert conditions:

# tests/blocklist.tftest.hcl

run "adds_wildcard_for_every_domain" {
  command = plan

  variables {
    vpc_id          = "vpc-0123456789abcdef0"
    blocked_domains = ["evil-domain.com", "definitely-not-crypto-mining.io"]
  }

  assert {
    condition     = length(aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_list.blocklist.domains) == 4
    error_message = "expected 2 domains + 2 wildcards, got ${length(aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_list.blocklist.domains)}"
  }

  assert {
    condition     = contains(aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_list.blocklist.domains, "*.evil-domain.com")
    error_message = "wildcard entry for evil-domain.com is missing"
  }
}

command = plan is the fast path. The module is planned, not applied, so anything that is known at plan time - which is most of what you would want to assert about your own logic - can be checked. Run it with tofu test from the module directory.

Even this much, with no mocking at all, already needs valid AWS credentials, because the provider is configured and some resources make API calls during plan. Which brings us to the point of this post.

mock_provider: no credentials, no API

Add a mock_provider block to the test file and the real AWS provider is never initialised:

mock_provider "aws" {}

run "adds_wildcard_for_every_domain" {
  command = plan
  # ... same as above
}

Every resource and data source of the mocked provider now returns made-up values for computed attributes: random strings for IDs and ARNs, and whatever you set in the configuration for the rest. No network, no AWS_PROFILE, runs on a laptop on a plane and in a GitHub Actions job with no secrets.

The made-up values are fine until a resource depends on a specific shape of a computed value. The rule group association needs the rule group’s id, and a random string works for that. But if your module has a regex() on an ARN, random garbage will not match. For those cases you tell the mock what to return:

mock_provider "aws" {
  mock_resource "aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group" {
    defaults = {
      id  = "rslvr-frg-0123456789abcdef0"
      arn = "arn:aws:route53resolver:eu-central-1:123456789012:firewall-rule-group/rslvr-frg-0123456789abcdef0"
    }
  }

  mock_data "aws_caller_identity" {
    defaults = {
      account_id = "123456789012"
    }
  }
}

mock_resource and mock_data set defaults per type. If you need a specific instance to return something, there is override_resource with a target, usable both inside mock_provider and at the top level of a run block.

command = apply, still without an account

With a mock provider you can also run command = apply. Nothing is created anywhere, the “apply” runs against the mock, but now attributes that are only known after apply are populated, so you can assert on outputs:

run "exposes_rule_group_id" {
  command = apply

  variables {
    vpc_id          = "vpc-0123456789abcdef0"
    blocked_domains = ["evil-domain.com"]
  }

  assert {
    condition     = startswith(output.rule_group_id, "rslvr-frg-")
    error_message = "rule_group_id output should be the firewall rule group id"
  }
}

This is the part that made the whole thing click for me. Apply-mode tests against a mock are what unit tests are for application code: fast, deterministic, no external state, and they catch the “I renamed the resource and forgot the output” class of bug immediately.

Testing that invalid input is rejected

The module has a validation block saying domains must not start with *. (the module adds wildcards itself). Test that the validation fires with expect_failures:

run "rejects_explicit_wildcards" {
  command = plan

  variables {
    vpc_id          = "vpc-0123456789abcdef0"
    blocked_domains = ["*.evil-domain.com"]
  }

  expect_failures = [
    var.blocked_domains,
  ]
}

The run passes only if that variable’s validation fails. If someone deletes the validation block, this test goes red.

Fixtures: a run block that sets things up

Sometimes a module needs an input that another module produces, a VPC for example. A run block can execute a different module and later runs can use its outputs:

run "setup" {
  module {
    source = "./tests/fixtures/vpc"
  }
}

run "attaches_to_the_vpc" {
  command = plan

  variables {
    vpc_id          = run.setup.vpc_id
    blocked_domains = ["evil-domain.com"]
  }

  assert {
    condition     = aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group_association.vpc.vpc_id == run.setup.vpc_id
    error_message = "association should target the fixture VPC"
  }
}

With a mock provider the fixture is also mocked, so it is still free. Against a real provider this is how you would do an integration test: real VPC up, module applied, assertions, everything destroyed at the end of the file - tofu test destroys what apply-mode runs created, in reverse order, even when an assertion fails.

In CI

- uses: opentofu/setup-opentofu@v1
- run: tofu init -backend=false
- run: tofu test
  working-directory: modules/dns-firewall

No AWS credentials in that job. The real-provider integration tests, if you have them, go in a separate workflow that runs on a schedule or on merge to main, with OIDC credentials, against a sandbox account.

What I would and would not test

Worth testing: your own logic - the for expressions, the locals, the conditionals, the validations, the outputs. That is where the bugs are and that is what mocks cover perfectly.

Not worth testing with mocks: whether AWS accepts the configuration. A mock will happily “create” a rule with action = "EXPLODE". For that you need the real provider, and one scheduled integration run is enough. The two layers together, mocked unit tests on every PR and a real apply nightly, is the first setup in years that made me stop being nervous about touching a shared module.
entry.summary: In July I published a DNS Firewall module and admitted that “tested” meant “applied it once and looked”. That is how most infrastructure modules are tested, and it is why module refactors are scary. OpenTofu has had tofu test since 1.6 and provider mocking since 1.8, which together let you assert what a module does - how many rules it creates, that the action is BLOCK, that the wildcard gets added - without credentials, without a VPC, in a few seconds, in CI. Here is that module with real tests.

entry.title: State surgery without the CLI: import, moved and removed blocks with for_each

link.title: State surgery without the CLI: import, moved and removed blocks with for_each

entry.content:
For about eight years, changing what is in the state meant typing terraform state mv and terraform import by hand, one resource at a time, in the right order, hoping nobody else ran an apply in between. Those commands still exist, but you should mostly stop using them. There are three declarative blocks - import, moved, removed - that do the same thing from code, show up in the plan, go through code review, and since they accept for_each they handle fifty resources as easily as one. This is in both OpenTofu and Terraform (since 1.7 on both sides), so unlike my last two posts this is not a “Tofu only” trick - it is a “most people still don’t use it” trick.

import: adopt existing infrastructure, in bulk

Somebody created twelve security groups in the console in 2019 and you are finally bringing them under management. The old way is twelve tofu import commands with twelve copy-pasted IDs. The new way:

variable "legacy_sgs" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    web      = "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001"
    api      = "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002"
    database = "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60003"
    # ... nine more
  }
}

import {
  for_each = var.legacy_sgs
  to       = aws_security_group.legacy[each.key]
  id       = each.value
}

resource "aws_security_group" "legacy" {
  for_each = var.legacy_sgs
  # ... attributes matching what exists
}

tofu plan now shows twelve “will be imported” lines next to any real changes. The import happens during apply, in the same run, under the same state lock. No separate step, no window where the state and the code disagree.

And you do not have to write the twelve resource bodies by hand either:

tofu plan -generate-config-out=legacy_sgs.tf

OpenTofu reads the real objects and writes a .tf file with their current attributes. The generated code is verbose and you will want to trim it (it writes every attribute, including defaults), but it beats reconstructing a security group from the console. Note that -generate-config-out only works for import blocks without for_each at the moment, so for bulk work generate once with a single block, turn it into a for_each resource yourself, and then switch the import block to for_each.

Once the apply is done, delete the import block. It has done its job and leaving it in produces a warning on every plan.

moved: rename and restructure without destroy/create

Every refactor that changes a resource address - renaming, wrapping in a module, going from count to for_each - used to mean a destroy and a recreate unless you remembered state mv. The moved block makes the refactor and the state change one commit:

# was: resource "aws_instance" "bastion" with count = 1
# now: module "bastion" with for_each over environments

moved {
  from = aws_instance.bastion[0]
  to   = module.bastion["prod"].aws_instance.this
}

moved does not take for_each, each move is explicit, but you can list as many as you need and they can chain (A moved to B in one release, B moved to C in the next, both blocks stay and OpenTofu follows the trail). It is the block I use most often and the one that has saved the most production instances from an accidental recreate. Keep moved blocks around for a few releases, then clean them up once you are sure every environment has applied them.

removed: forget a resource without destroying it

The opposite of import. You want OpenTofu to stop managing something but keep the thing itself - handing a bucket over to another team’s state, or a resource you are going to manage with a different tool. Previously: tofu state rm, which is a direct state edit with no plan and no review. Now:

removed {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.handed_over

  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}

With destroy = false the plan says “will no longer be managed” and the bucket stays. Without it, removed behaves like deleting the resource block, which is to say it destroys. That default surprises people, so I would make a habit of always writing the lifecycle block, even when destroy is what you want, so the intent is in the diff.

removed also does not take for_each, but from can point at a whole resource including all its instances (from = aws_s3_bucket.handed_over covers every [key]), and at a module (from = module.legacy), which in practice covers the bulk cases.

Putting it together: the three-step refactor

A pattern that comes up constantly - a module that was copy-pasted per environment gets collapsed into one for_each module. The sequence that works, all in code, all in review:

# 1. new shape
module "app" {
  for_each = toset(["dev", "staging", "prod"])
  source   = "./modules/app"
  env      = each.key
}

# 2. moves from the old addresses
moved {
  from = module.app_dev
  to   = module.app["dev"]
}
moved {
  from = module.app_staging
  to   = module.app["staging"]
}
moved {
  from = module.app_prod
  to   = module.app["prod"]
}

# 3. adopt the one thing that was never in state
import {
  to = module.app["prod"].aws_cloudwatch_log_group.this
  id = "/aws/app/prod"
}

Plan shows three moves and one import and zero destroys. If it shows a destroy, you got an address wrong, and you find that out before anything happens rather than after.

What the CLI is still for

tofu state mv, rm, import are not deprecated and they are still the right tool for emergency surgery - a broken state after an interrupted apply, a one-off fix at 2 a.m. For everything planned, the blocks are strictly better: they are reviewable, they run under the lock, they are idempotent (applying a moved twice is a no-op), and with for_each on import they scale. The mental shift is small: state changes are code changes now, and they go through the same pipeline as everything else.

entry.title: OpenTofu state encryption: encrypt an existing state and rotate the key without downtime

link.title: OpenTofu state encryption: encrypt an existing state and rotate the key without downtime

entry.content:
Your state file has your database password in it. Not a hash, not a reference, the password. Also every secret the AWS provider ever returned, every private key you generated with the tls provider, every random_password. S3 bucket encryption does not help here, because anyone who can read the bucket gets the plaintext back from S3. OpenTofu 1.7 added client-side state encryption: the state is encrypted before it leaves your machine and S3 only ever sees ciphertext. This post is the practical part - turning it on for an existing project, and then rotating the key - because the docs explain the blocks but not the sequence.

The three building blocks

Everything lives in a new encryption block inside terraform {}. Three kinds of things inside:

  • a key_provider - where the key comes from (a passphrase, AWS KMS, GCP KMS, OpenBao),
  • a method - how the key is used (aes_gcm is the one you want),
  • and the targets - state and plan, each pointing at a method.

A minimal AWS setup looks like this:

terraform {
  encryption {
    key_provider "aws_kms" "main" {
      kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:eu-central-1:123456789012:key/0123abcd-..."
      region     = "eu-central-1"
      key_spec   = "AES_256"
    }

    method "aes_gcm" "main" {
      keys = key_provider.aws_kms.main
    }

    state {
      method = method.aes_gcm.main
    }

    plan {
      method = method.aes_gcm.main
    }
  }
}

On every write OpenTofu asks KMS for a fresh data key (GenerateDataKey), encrypts the state with it locally, and stores the encrypted data key next to the ciphertext. On read it asks KMS to unwrap that data key. So the IAM permission you need on the key is kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt, nothing else. The key material never leaves KMS, the plaintext state never leaves your process. Plan files get the same treatment, which matters more than people think - a saved plan contains the full proposed state, secrets included.

If you do not have KMS, a passphrase works too:

key_provider "pbkdf2" "main" {
  passphrase = var.state_passphrase   # at least 16 characters
}

Sensitive variable, fed from CI secrets. Fine for a personal project, not what I would pick for a team because now you have a shared secret to rotate and no audit trail of who used it.

Turning it on for a project that already has state

This is where people get stuck. You add the block above, run tofu plan, and it fails: OpenTofu tries to decrypt the existing state, which is plaintext, and refuses. It will not silently guess.

The answer is a fallback. The state block can carry a second method that is only used for reading. Writing always uses the primary method. So the migration is: primary = encrypted, fallback = unencrypted, apply once, remove the fallback.

terraform {
  encryption {
    key_provider "aws_kms" "main" { ... }

    method "aes_gcm" "main" {
      keys = key_provider.aws_kms.main
    }

    method "unencrypted" "migrate" {}

    state {
      method = method.aes_gcm.main
      fallback {
        method = method.unencrypted.migrate
      }
    }
  }
}

Run tofu apply (an empty apply with no changes is enough, OpenTofu rewrites the state on every apply). Pull the state with tofu state pull - if it worked you now see a JSON document with an encrypted_data field and base64 garbage instead of your resources. Then delete the unencrypted method and the fallback, and add one more line:

state {
  method   = method.aes_gcm.main
  enforced = true
}

enforced = true means “refuse to ever read or write unencrypted state”. Without it, a colleague who checks out an old commit without the encryption block can still accidentally write plaintext back. With it, OpenTofu errors out instead. Turn it on as soon as the migration is done, and consider it part of the migration, not an optional extra.

Rotating the key

Same trick, other direction. New key becomes primary, old key becomes fallback, apply, drop the fallback:

key_provider "aws_kms" "old" {
  kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:eu-central-1:123456789012:key/0123abcd-..."
  region     = "eu-central-1"
  key_spec   = "AES_256"
}

key_provider "aws_kms" "new" {
  kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:eu-central-1:123456789012:key/4567ef01-..."
  region     = "eu-central-1"
  key_spec   = "AES_256"
}

method "aes_gcm" "old" { keys = key_provider.aws_kms.old }
method "aes_gcm" "new" { keys = key_provider.aws_kms.new }

state {
  method   = method.aes_gcm.new
  enforced = true
  fallback {
    method = method.aes_gcm.old
  }
}

One apply per state file, and the data is re-encrypted under the new key. Keep the old KMS key around until every state that was ever encrypted with it has been rewritten - including the ones in that one workspace nobody has touched since spring. Then schedule it for deletion. Note that with KMS you rarely need to rotate the customer master key yourself, KMS can rotate the backing material automatically and old ciphertexts stay decryptable. The procedure above is for when you actually want to move to a different key, say from a shared one to a per-project one.

The bits that bite

terraform_remote_state from another project. If project B reads A’s state with the terraform_remote_state data source, B needs to be able to decrypt it. There is a dedicated block for that:

encryption {
  remote_state_data_sources {
    default {
      method = method.aes_gcm.main
    }
  }
}

Forget it and B fails with a decryption error that mentions nothing about remote state.

CI. You probably do not want the key configuration duplicated in every root module. The whole encryption block can be supplied through the TF_ENCRYPTION environment variable as HCL or JSON, and it is merged with what is in the code. One variable in your CI secrets, no key ARNs scattered across repos.

Terraform cannot read it anymore. Obvious, but worth saying out loud: once the state is encrypted, terraform and every tool that parses state directly (some policy scanners, some cost tools, your own jq scripts) sees only the envelope. tofu state pull and tofu show -json still give you plaintext because they decrypt on the way out, so pipe through those instead of reading the S3 object.

Lock the config. The encryption block is code, so a PR can remove enforced = true. Code review is the control here; put the encryption config in a file that your CODEOWNERS routes to the platform team.

Is it worth it

For a solo project with a private S3 bucket and no secrets in state - probably not, it is one more moving part. For anything where several people and a CI system can read the bucket, I think it is the single cheapest security improvement available in the whole toolchain: an afternoon, one KMS key, zero changes to the resources themselves, and the “state file leaked” incident class is gone. It is also, as far as I can tell, the feature where OpenTofu is furthest ahead of Terraform, which has had the “encrypt state at rest, client side” issue open since 2014.

entry.title: One module block, every region: provider for_each in OpenTofu

link.title: One module block, every region: provider for_each in OpenTofu

entry.content:
Here is a thing I wish somebody had shown me the week OpenTofu 1.9 came out. If you have ever had to deploy the same stack to five AWS regions, you know the ritual: five provider "aws" blocks with five aliases, five copies of the module block differing only in the providers map, and a bad feeling every time a sixth region shows up. In OpenTofu you can put for_each on the provider block itself. One provider block, one module block, regions come from a variable. Terraform still cannot do this.

The old way, for contrast

This is what multi-region looked like in every repo I have worked in:

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "frankfurt"
  region = "eu-central-1"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "ireland"
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "virginia"
  region = "us-east-1"
}

module "dns_firewall_frankfurt" {
  source    = "./modules/dns-firewall"
  providers = { aws = aws.frankfurt }
  vpc_id    = var.vpc_ids["eu-central-1"]
}

module "dns_firewall_ireland" {
  source    = "./modules/dns-firewall"
  providers = { aws = aws.ireland }
  vpc_id    = var.vpc_ids["eu-west-1"]
}

module "dns_firewall_virginia" {
  source    = "./modules/dns-firewall"
  providers = { aws = aws.virginia }
  vpc_id    = var.vpc_ids["us-east-1"]
}

Three regions, and already nobody wants to touch it. People reach for templating (cookiecutter, a Python script spitting out .tf files, Terragrunt) and now the infrastructure code has a build step. All of that because provider blocks could not be iterated.

The OpenTofu way

Since OpenTofu 1.9:

variable "regions" {
  type    = set(string)
  default = ["eu-central-1", "eu-west-1", "us-east-1"]
}

variable "vpc_ids" {
  type = map(string)
}

provider "aws" {
  alias    = "by_region"
  for_each = var.regions
  region   = each.value
}

module "dns_firewall" {
  source   = "./modules/dns-firewall"
  for_each = var.regions

  providers = {
    aws = aws.by_region[each.key]
  }

  vpc_id = var.vpc_ids[each.key]
}

That is the whole trick. aws.by_region is now a map of provider instances keyed by region, and aws.by_region[each.key] hands the right one to each module instance. Adding a region is adding a string to a set. The module code inside ./modules/dns-firewall did not change at all, it still just says provider "aws" and gets whatever it is given.

It works on resources too, not only modules, in case you do not want a module for a three-resource thing:

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "dns_firewall" {
  for_each = var.regions
  provider = aws.by_region[each.key]

  name              = "/aws/route53resolver/dns-firewall"
  retention_in_days = 30
}

Why this was impossible before: early evaluation

The reason Terraform never did this is not laziness, it is the evaluation model. Provider configuration has to be known before the graph is built, because providers are what the graph talks to. Anything in a provider block had to be a literal or a variable with no dependencies.

OpenTofu 1.8 introduced what the docs call early evaluation (you will also see “static evaluation”): variables and locals that can be resolved before the graph exists are allowed in places that used to be literal-only. Provider for_each in 1.9 is built on top of it. The same mechanism gives you two other things advanced users have been asking for since roughly 2015:

# a variable in the backend config
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = var.state_bucket
    key    = "dns-firewall/${var.environment}.tfstate"
    region = "eu-central-1"
  }
}

# a variable in a module source
module "dns_firewall" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/example/tofu-modules.git//dns-firewall?ref=${var.modules_ref}"
  # ...
}

The rule to remember: the value has to be knowable without talking to any provider. Variables, locals built from variables, functions on those - fine. Anything that comes out of a data source or a resource - no, and OpenTofu tells you so at plan time, not with a cryptic error halfway through apply.

The gotcha, and the pattern that avoids it

There is one sharp edge, and it is the same one aliased providers always had, just easier to hit now. Say you remove us-east-1 from var.regions. OpenTofu now wants to destroy module.dns_firewall["us-east-1"], but the provider instance aws.by_region["us-east-1"] is gone from the configuration too, and you cannot destroy a resource without the provider that created it. Plan fails.

The fix is to decouple the two sets. Providers iterate over every region you could ever have, modules iterate over the ones you actually want right now:

locals {
  # every region this account is ever allowed to touch
  all_regions = ["eu-central-1", "eu-west-1", "eu-north-1", "us-east-1", "us-west-2"]
}

variable "active_regions" {
  type    = set(string)
  default = ["eu-central-1", "eu-west-1"]
}

provider "aws" {
  alias    = "by_region"
  for_each = toset(local.all_regions)
  region   = each.value
}

module "dns_firewall" {
  source   = "./modules/dns-firewall"
  for_each = var.active_regions
  providers = { aws = aws.by_region[each.key] }
  vpc_id   = var.vpc_ids[each.key]
}

Now removing a region from active_regions produces a clean destroy, because the provider instance for it still exists. An unused provider instance costs nothing, it is just configuration. Add a validation block on active_regions checking setsubtract(var.active_regions, local.all_regions) is empty if you want a friendlier error than the one OpenTofu gives for a missing map key.

Two small bonuses

Since the module instances are keyed by region, you can do one region at a time without touching the code. OpenTofu 1.9 also added -exclude, the mirror image of -target:

# roll out only Frankfurt first
tofu apply -target='module.dns_firewall["eu-central-1"]'

# everything except Virginia, which is in the middle of an incident
tofu apply -exclude='module.dns_firewall["us-east-1"]'

And because the region is each.key, your outputs come out as a map for free:

output "rule_group_ids" {
  value = { for region, m in module.dns_firewall : region => m.rule_group_id }
}

Should you migrate existing code to this?

If you have the five-copies setup and it works, the honest answer is: only when you touch it next. The addresses change from module.dns_firewall_frankfurt to module.dns_firewall["eu-central-1"], so you need a moved block per region or a state move, which is a chore but a one-time one. For anything new, I do not see a reason to write the old pattern ever again. Requires OpenTofu 1.9 or newer, and the provider itself does not have to know or care.

If you have ever had to deploy the same stack to five AWS regions, you know the ritual: five provider "aws" blocks with five aliases, five copies of the module block differing only in the providers map, and a bad feeling every time a sixth region shows up. In OpenTofu you can put for_each on the provider block itself. One provider block, one module block, regions come from a variable. Terraform still cannot do this.

entry.title: I turned this blog into a terminal window (and threw out the theme while I was at it)

link.title: I turned this blog into a terminal window (and threw out the theme while I was at it)

entry.content:
So, new look. If you were here before you probably remember a white page with a serif font that looked like every other Jekyll blog from 2016 - because that is exactly what it was. I have wanted something that looks like the thing I stare at all day for a long time, and last evening I finally did it. This is a short note on how, mostly because I ended up deleting more than I added, and that part surprised me.

How it started

I did not start from a design. I started from a complaint: the old theme pulled in a Google font, Font Awesome (the whole 30 KB of it, for three icons in the footer) and a theme gem I had not updated in years. For a blog that is ninety percent text and HCL snippets. Every time I touched it I had the feeling I was maintaining someone else’s furniture.

Then the “make it look like a console” idea came back, and I decided the two problems have one solution: rip out the theme, write the layouts myself, and keep only what I can read in one sitting.

I was lazy about it, in the good way. I had Claude Code throw together three static mockups - a green-on-black retro one with scanlines, a dark “modern terminal” one, and a man-page style light one - opened them side by side and picked. The retro one was the most fun and the least readable. The man page was the most readable and did not look like a terminal at all. The middle one won, with the scanlines stolen from the retro one because I liked them too much to let go.

What is actually there now

Six layout files in _layouts/, two tiny includes, one CSS file. No framework, no JavaScript in the theme, no web fonts - it uses whatever monospace and sans fonts your system already has. The icons became words. Turns out “GitHub” written as a word is perfectly understandable.

The whole page sits in a fake window, about 128 characters wide, which is roughly how wide I keep my real terminal:

.win{position:relative;max-width:128ch;margin:0 auto;background:#1e1e2e;
     border-radius:10px;border:1px solid #313244;box-shadow:0 20px 60px rgba(0,0,0,.5);overflow:hidden}
.bar{background:#313244;padding:.55rem 1rem;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:.45rem}
.bar i{width:12px;height:12px;border-radius:50%}
.bar i:nth-child(1){background:#f38ba8}.bar i:nth-child(2){background:#f9e2af}.bar i:nth-child(3){background:#a6e3a1}

The three dots in the title bar are three empty <i> tags with a background colour. I was half expecting to need an SVG for that, nope.

Colours are Catppuccin Mocha. Not a deep decision - it is everywhere already, it is easy on the eyes, and giscus has a theme with the same name, so the comments box below the posts does not look like someone glued a white sticker on a dark screen.

The prompt thing

Every page is a sequence of fake commands and their “output”. The prompt is a Jekyll include, I pass it the directory and the command:

<div class="p"><span class="arrow">➜</span> <span class="h">robert@notes</span>
<span class="d">{{ include.cwd }}</span> <span class="g">git:(</span><span class="arrow">master</span><span class="g">)</span>
<span class="c">{{ include.cmd }}</span></div>

The front page pretends to run ls -t posts/ | head -n 5 | xargs head -n 3, a post is glow something.md, the archive is ls -lt, a tag page is grep -l "tag: AWS" *.md. Yes, it is a gag. But it is a gag that also tells you where on the site you are, so I am keeping it.

Blinking cursor and scanlines, no JS

I was sure the cursor would need a few lines of JavaScript. It does not, it is a pseudo-element with a one-step animation. Same for the scanlines, that is a repeating gradient painted over the window. The important bit is pointer-events: none, otherwise you cannot select text through it - I learned that one the hard way, about thirty seconds after adding it.

.cur::after{content:"▋";animation:bl 1.1s steps(1) infinite}
@keyframes bl{50%{opacity:0}}
@media(prefers-reduced-motion:reduce){.cur::after{animation:none}}

.win::after{content:"";position:absolute;inset:0;pointer-events:none;
  background:repeating-linear-gradient(0deg,rgba(0,0,0,.12) 0 1px,transparent 1px 3px)}

The prefers-reduced-motion line is there because a blinking thing in the corner is cute for me and genuinely unpleasant for some people. One line, do it.

The one real decision: not everything is monospace

This is the part I went back and forth on. A page that is 100% monospace looks the most like a terminal. It is also tiring to read once a post goes past a few hundred words, and some of mine go well past that. So I split it: anything that is “UI” - prompts, nav, titles, headings, code - is monospace, and the body text of a post is a normal sans font, slightly bigger. Headings keep a ## in front of them, drawn by CSS, so they still look like markdown in a terminal:

.post .body{font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,"Segoe UI",Roboto,sans-serif;font-size:1.03rem;line-height:1.7}
.post .body h2{font-family:ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;color:#cba6f7}
.post .body h2::before{content:"## ";color:#6c7086}

If you are reading this on the site, you are looking at the result. If it bugs you, tell me, the mono-everything version is one CSS rule away.

A small confession

The theme has no JavaScript, but the page does. Google Analytics is still here, the comments are giscus (so that is an iframe plus a script on post pages), and the contact form still has reCAPTCHA in front of it. Same three third parties as before, I just moved the furniture around them. I did briefly have “no JS, no cookies” in the footer, noticed it was a lie, and took it out. Whether to actually go cookie-free is a question for another evening.

Was it worth it

Byte-wise, not dramatically: the stylesheet went from about 10 KB to about 7, and the font and icon downloads went to zero. The site was never heavy. What I got rid of is moving parts. There is no theme gem to keep compatible with Jekyll anymore, no CDN link that can rot, nothing to update. Seventy lines of CSS, and I know what every one of them does. For a blog I post to a couple of times a year, that is the right amount of frontend to own.

entry.title: Claude Code skills - teach the agent your workflow once, in a Markdown file

link.title: Claude Code skills - teach the agent your workflow once, in a Markdown file

entry.content:
Every time I opened Claude Code I was typing the same paragraph: “new post goes to _posts, file name starts with the date, front matter looks like this, build to a temp dir, don’t touch docs/”. Then I discovered that this paragraph has a proper home. It is called a skill, it is one Markdown file, and the agent loads it on its own when the task matches. This post is the five minute version: what a skill is, where it lives, and two examples worth copying.

What a skill is

A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md inside. The file has a small YAML front matter and then plain instructions:

---
name: post
description: Create a new blog post for this Jekyll blog. Use when asked to write, draft or scaffold a post.
---

Create a new post in `_posts/`.

1. File name: `YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.markdown`, today's date, slug from the title.
2. Front matter exactly like the existing posts: `layout: post`, quoted `title`,
   `date` with `+02:00`, `tag` as a list, single `category`.
3. First paragraph is the excerpt, then `<!--more-->`, then the body.
4. Build with `bundle exec jekyll build -d /tmp/site` and report errors. Never write to `docs/`.

Title and topic: $ARGUMENTS

Two things matter here. The description is the trigger - Claude reads it to decide whether the skill applies, so write it as “what it does + when to use it”, like a search query you would type yourself. $ARGUMENTS is whatever you type after the slash command, so /post Route 53 DNS Firewall with OpenTofu lands in the last line.

Where it lives

Location Scope
~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md you, every project
.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md this repository, committed, shared with the team

The project variant is the interesting one for teams. The runbook for “how we cut a release” or “how we review a module” stops being tribal knowledge in someone’s head and becomes a file in the repo that both humans and the agent read.

How it gets used

Two ways. You type /post ... and it runs. Or you just say “write a post about X” and Claude picks the skill because the description matches. Until that moment only the name and description sit in the context, the body is loaded on demand. That is why you can have dozens of skills without paying for them on every request.

If a skill is dangerous enough that you never want it auto-selected - deploy, anything touching production - add disable-model-invocation: true to the front matter. Then only the explicit slash command triggers it.

Supporting files

A skill directory can hold more than SKILL.md: a scripts/ folder with a shell or Python helper, a references/ folder with a long checklist or an API cheat sheet. Reference them from SKILL.md by relative path and they are read only when needed. Rule of thumb that worked for me: keep SKILL.md short enough to read in one screen, move anything longer into a reference file.

A second one for the infrastructure repo

An OpenTofu review checklist, project-scoped, so every reviewer and the agent use the same list:

---
name: tofu-review
description: Review OpenTofu/Terraform changes. Use when asked to review .tf files, a module or a plan output.
---

Review the changed `.tf` files against this list and report findings as file:line bullets, worst first:

- resources without `lifecycle { prevent_destroy }` where data would be lost (RDS, S3, EBS, KMS),
- `count = cond ? 1 : 0` on a resource that already exists in state - needs a `moved` block,
- provider versions not pinned with `~>`,
- IAM policies with `"Action": "*"` or `"Resource": "*"`,
- security groups open to `0.0.0.0/0` on anything but 80/443,
- hardcoded account IDs, regions or ARNs that should be data sources or variables.

Do not run `tofu plan` or `tofu apply`. `tofu fmt -check` and `tofu validate` are fine.

Nothing clever. It is the same list I would go through by hand, except now I do not forget point four at 17:55 on a Friday.

Skill, CLAUDE.md or subagent?

  • CLAUDE.md is loaded always. Put there what applies to every single request: coding conventions, “never run apply”, commit message rules. Keep it short, you pay for it every time.
  • A skill is loaded when relevant. Put there a workflow, a checklist, a procedure.
  • A subagent is a separate context with its own tools. Reach for it when the task is big enough to pollute your main conversation, like reading forty files to answer one question.

Most of what I used to stuff into CLAUDE.md turned out to be skills.

Three mistakes to skip

  1. Vague description. “Helpful blog utilities” gives the model nothing to match on. “Create a new blog post for this Jekyll blog. Use when asked to write, draft or scaffold a post.” does.
  2. Skill that does too much. One skill that wrote, built, committed and deployed. Split it: /post writes and builds, deploy is a separate skill with disable-model-invocation: true.
  3. No test. After writing a skill, ask for the task without naming the skill. If Claude does not pick it up, the description is wrong, not the model.

That is the whole thing. One directory, one Markdown file, a good description.
